event: UFC Fight Night: Nurmagomedov vs. Song
venue: Shanghai Oriental Sports Center, Shanghai, China

items.fight_news: Umar Nurmagomedov headlines in a five-round bantamweight main event with a 20-1 record and one of the division's strongest control games. His only loss came in top-tier company, so this booking works as a fast test of whether he can reassert title-contender status without taking a softer reset fight.

Song Yadong gets a home-country main event in Shanghai with a 23-9-1 record and years of UFC experience against ranked bantamweights. The crowd angle is real here: Song is not just protecting his place in the division, he is carrying the card's biggest local spotlight.

The broad public read is grappling pressure against fast boxing. Nurmagomedov is expected to threaten level changes and positional control, while Song's clearest appeal is speed, power, and the ability to turn one clean exchange into momentum in front of a favorable crowd.

Five rounds make this more than a simple style clash. Song has to manage long stretches where defending takedowns can cost energy even when he stays upright, while Nurmagomedov has to prove he can keep winning minutes if the first few entries meet real resistance.

Yan Xiaonan enters the co-feature slot as the established Chinese strawweight name at 19-5. Her presence gives the Shanghai card a second major local hook, and a win would keep her visible in a division where a familiar contender can move quickly with one strong performance.

Denise Gomes brings a 12-3 record and a more compact, aggressive style profile into a difficult road assignment. She is the less locally celebrated fighter, but her pressure and willingness to exchange make her a dangerous opponent for a cleaner technician.

For public users, the story is experience and home support against physical urgency. Yan has seen longer elite-level fights, while Gomes can change the feel of the bout if she forces messy pocket exchanges before Yan settles into range.

Aoriqileng carries a 26-13 record into a bantamweight main-card fight that should draw local interest. He has been a familiar action fighter for UFC audiences, and this setting gives him a chance to turn crowd energy into a notable late-career moment.

Kai Asakura enters at 22-6 with major Japanese name value and a reputation for explosive offense. He is not being eased into an anonymous undercard spot; this placement asks whether his power and timing can translate against a tough, experienced opponent.

This bout has a simple fan-friendly setup: Aoriqileng is durable and willing to trade, while Asakura is the sharper finisher when exchanges open. That mix makes early momentum important because both men are comfortable in high-contact stretches.

Alex Perez brings the deeper UFC resume and a 26-10 record into this flyweight main-card matchup. He has spent years near high-level opposition, which gives this fight a veteran-versus-home-region angle rather than a pure prospect test.

Sumudaerji is 19-7 and gives the Shanghai audience another Chinese fighter in a prominent card position. His striking-first reputation makes him an easy fighter for casual users to track, especially if he can keep the fight in open space.

The basic stakes are divisional relevance and style control. Perez has more proven wrestling and all-around experience, while Sumudaerji's best public-facing route is distance striking and making the fight feel like a kickboxing match.

Ce Liu is listed at 3-1 in a light heavyweight main-card matchup, giving him a fast visibility jump on a China-based UFC card. That kind of placement can accelerate a fighter's profile quickly if he looks composed under the bigger broadcast spotlight.

Junior Tafa enters at 7-6 and is the more familiar UFC name to many viewers because of his heavyweight and light heavyweight appearances. His record is uneven, but his power and willingness to engage make him dangerous against a less tested opponent.

This is a placement-driven opportunity for Liu and a reset chance for Tafa. The public angle is straightforward: Liu gets the local-stage upside, while Tafa brings known finishing threat and experience in bigger athletes' exchanges.

Bilal Hasan and Nilson Rojas are both listed at 9-0, making this flyweight bout one of the cleanest undefeated-versus-undefeated fights on the card. Even without major name recognition, that record pairing gives users an easy reason to watch closely.

Hasan represents Indonesia and Rojas represents Chile, adding an international prospect angle to the main card. For a lower-weight fight in this slot, a clear win can matter because flyweight often rewards fighters who immediately show pace, confidence, and finishing ambition.

The matchup carries natural uncertainty because neither fighter has a loss on the public ledger. The first round should tell casual viewers who is more comfortable when the opponent does not back down from an unbeaten record.

Namsrai Batbayar opens the ESPN-listed prelim slate at 9-1 against a strong flyweight opponent. His Mongolian flag and record give this fight regional interest on an Asia card, especially because a win over Andre Lima would be a meaningful resume step.

Andre Lima is 11-1 and has already built a reputation as a powerful flyweight. He enters as the more familiar name to many UFC viewers, and his ability to make small-weight-class fights feel physically damaging is the obvious public hook.

This is one of the better prelim fights for prediction users because both fighters have strong records and clear forward momentum. The winner can leave Shanghai with a much stronger argument for a more visible flyweight assignment.

Rei Tsuruya comes in at 11-1 and remains one of Japan's notable flyweight names on this card. His placement on the prelims keeps the pressure lower than a main-card slot, but the regional spotlight still makes this an important performance window.

Kevin Borjas is 11-5 and gives Tsuruya an opponent with enough experience to make the fight more than a showcase. Borjas has been around high-level flyweight matchups, so his value here is making Tsuruya prove control rather than just promise.

Jack Jenkins brings a 14-4 record into a featherweight prelim against one of the longest frames in the division. He has already been through UFC-level tempo, and this matchup gives him a chance to rebuild momentum against a recognizable opponent.

Sean Woodson is 13-2-1 and remains a difficult style assignment because of his height, reach, and volume at featherweight. The public story is whether Jenkins can get inside often enough or whether Woodson keeps the fight at his preferred long range.

Xiao Long enters at 27-11 and adds another Chinese fighter to the Shanghai prelims. His experience level is high for this part of the card, which makes the bout useful for users who value record depth over prospect shine.

Francesco Nuzzi is listed at 11-2 and brings Italy into the bantamweight matchup. The fight has a classic road-underdog feel: Nuzzi needs to show that his cleaner record can travel against a veteran with local crowd support.

Lawrence Lui is 8-1 and gets a bantamweight prelim slot representing New Zealand. This is the kind of fight where a young record can gain value quickly, because a composed UFC-card win matters more than raw numbers alone.

Hector Santiago enters at 6-1 from Brazil, giving the fight a prospect-versus-prospect shape. With both fighters carrying only one listed loss, the result should tell users more about readiness than name value.

Jingnan Xiong is listed at 19-3 and brings major Chinese combat-sports recognition to the UFC strawweight prelims. Even lower on the bout order, her name gives the card a significant local-interest piece beyond the headliner.

Julia Polastri is 14-6 and has the role of experienced spoiler against a highly recognizable opponent. The public angle is clear: Polastri can disrupt a local showcase if she turns the fight into a hard, practical three-round test.

This fight matters for more than placement because Xiong's broader reputation can create immediate expectations. A strong UFC performance in Shanghai would make her a much easier athlete for casual users to track going forward.

Ding Meng is listed with a 35-10 record, the deepest pro ledger on the card by total fights. That experience gives the welterweight prelim a veteran angle, especially on a China-hosted event where his name can still stand out early.

Cameron Nelson enters at 7-1 and brings a much shorter but cleaner record. The public-facing read is volume of experience against fresher upside, a contrast that often makes early composure the first thing to watch.
